clean_story:
"Automatic entrances. Hands-free access.

The name sliding doors comes from their motion—panels glide sideways on tracks instead of swinging open like a gate. Most see them as convenience, yet their design hides a balance: weight, speed, and silence. A typical system uses a motor, pulleys, and a counterweight to move panels weighing up to 400 kilograms with minimal effort, like a drawer sliding on well-oiled rails. Sensors detect motion within a 3-meter range, triggering the mechanism in under a second. In hospitals, they prevent germ spread by eliminating door handles. In airports, they handle 10,000 daily passages without wear. The precision lies in the threshold—the gap between panels must stay below 6 millimeters to block drafts yet avoid pinching. Early models in the 1950s used manual push; today’s versions sync with fire alarms to unlock instantly during emergencies.

Three related subjects are motion sensors, automatic gates, and silent machinery."
